channel.title: The Prototype
channel.description: Every week, The Prototype takes you inside the tech being built right now — the breakthroughs, the wild experiments, and the quiet revolutions that will shape the next decade. No hype, no jargon walls, just the amazing stuff explained straight. The future is already under construction. Come watch it get built.

item.title: The Prototype #13: The Dry Copy: How Chester Carlson's Kitchen Experiment Built Xerox
item.description: In 1938, a patent clerk melted sulfur on his kitchen stove until it caught fire and stank up the house, chasing an idea every expert called impossible: making copies with no wet chemistry at all. Twenty-one companies turned Chester Carlson down. Then his dry-copy machine became the Xerox 914, the most successful product ever marketed in America. Alden Isaac traces how xerography went from a handkerchief-rubbed zinc plate in a Queens beauty parlor back room to the machine that built the modern office: the sulfur fires, the lycopodium powder, the selenium drum breakthrough, the hotel unveiling where one copier caught fire on live television, and the 95-dollar-a-month rental plan that turned Xerox into a verb. Cover photo: the Xerox 914 itself, photo by Marcin Wichary, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: The Prototype #12: Black and White Squares: How the QR Code Took Over the World
item.description: In 1994, a Denso Wave engineer named Masahiro Hara stared at a barcode and saw its limits: twenty characters, one direction only. So he built a square that could hold thousands of characters, be read from any angle, and survive damage. Then he gave it away for free. Alden Isaac traces how the QR code went from tracking car parts to menus, payments, and tickets everywhere: the finder patterns, the error correction that reads through damage, and the decision not to patent it that let it take over the world. Cover photo: portrait by the Japan Academy, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: The Prototype #11: The Booster That Came Back: How Rockets Learned to Land
item.description: For decades, rockets were trash: you flew them once and threw them away. Then one December night in 2015, a booster came back down and landed standing up. Alden Isaac traces how rockets learned to land: the DC-X experiments, the Shuttle's broken economics, the Grasshopper test flights, the first touchdown, the droneship catches, and the chopstick arms now grabbing Starship out of the sky. Cover photo: SpaceX, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

item.title: The Prototype #10: The Little Switch: How the Transistor Rewired the World
item.description: In 1947, a sliver of germanium smaller than a postage stamp did something no vacuum tube could: it amplified a signal without heat, without burnouts, without warming up. Alden Isaac traces how John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley invented the transistor at Bell Labs: the forgotten 1920s patents, the surface-state breakthrough, the December experiment that carried a human voice, and how that tiny switch rewired the world. Cover photo: Bell Labs publicity photo, 1948, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

item.title: The Prototype #9: The Radar Kitchen: How a Melted Candy Bar Invented the Microwave Oven
item.description: An engineer at Raytheon leans against a running radar magnetron and feels something strange in his pocket: his candy bar has melted. Alden Isaac traces how Percy Spencer, a man with a fifth-grade education, turned that moment into the microwave oven: the war-born magnetron, the six-foot-tall, thousand-pound Radarange, and the long road from military hardware to the box humming in your kitchen. Cover photo: Acroterion, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Music: Bach's Air on the G String, performed by the United States Air Force Strings (public domain).

item.title: The Prototype #8: Hands on the Keyboard: How AI Learned to Do Things
item.description: A developer in Berlin types one paragraph describing a bug, goes to make coffee, and comes back to find the fix written, tested, and submitted for her review. Alden Isaac traces how AI learned to do things instead of just saying them: the mechanical trick that gave models hands, the coding agents ninety percent of professional developers now use every week, and what happens when software stops answering questions and starts doing the work. Music: Bach's Air on the G String, performed by the United States Air Force Strings (public domain).

item.title: The Prototype #7: The Fire Below: The Frackers Drilling for Endless Clean Power
item.description: The hottest new idea in clean energy comes from the oilfield. Alden Isaac goes inside enhanced geothermal: the fracking crews drilling miles down to crack hot dry rock, the startups turning earthquakes into engineering, and the race to make endless clean power as cheap as dirt. Cover photo: Rjglewis, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: The Prototype #6: Bottled Lightning: How the Lithium Battery Took Over the World
item.description: A battery in Poland big enough to carry half a million homes through an evening. Alden Isaac traces how the lithium battery went from lab curiosity to the engine of the modern world: the chemistry breakthroughs, the stunning price crash, the gigafactories rising in deserts, and the race for whatever comes next. Cover photo: Smnt, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

item.title: The Prototype #5: Light on the Ocean Floor: The Cables That Carry the Internet
item.description: Ninety-nine percent of intercontinental internet traffic travels as light through glass threads on the ocean floor. Alden Isaac goes inside the undersea cable network: the Victorian dreamer who wired the Atlantic, the repair ships that fix four breaks a week, the Baltic sabotage gray zone, and why Meta is spending billions to lay its own private highway across the planet. Cover photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Music: "Deliberate Thought" by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), licensed under CC BY 3.0.

item.title: The Prototype #4: The Box That Shrank the World: The Truck Driver Who Rebuilt Global Trade
item.description: In March of twenty twenty-one, the Ever Given wedged itself into the Suez Canal and one stuck ship held up ten billion dollars a day in goods. All of it packed inside the same boring steel box. This is the story of the shipping container: the most important invention of the twentieth century, hiding in plain sight, invented by a truck driver who got tired of waiting at a dock. How a simple steel box rebuilt global trade, shrank the world, and put your phone, your shoes, and your coffee on a ship across the ocean. Cover photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

item.title: The Prototype #3: Carving Light: The Machine That Prints the Modern World
item.description: Every advanced chip on Earth is printed by a single machine built by a single Dutch company. Alden Isaac goes inside extreme ultraviolet lithography: vaporizing tin with lasers to make light that barely exists in nature, mirrors smoother than anything else on Earth, and the twenty-year bet the experts ranked dead last. Cover photo: ASML.

item.title: The Prototype #2: Your Phone Is Doing Relativity: The Hidden Genius of GPS
item.description: Your phone's blue dot is drawn by atomic clocks flying twelve thousand six hundred miles overhead, clocks deliberately set wrong at the factory to account for Einstein's relativity. In this episode of The Prototype, Alden Isaac goes inside GPS: the four-satellite math trick, the thirty-eight microsecond drift, the tragedy that opened it to the world, and how a military navigation system quietly became the heartbeat of modern civilization.

item.title: The Prototype #1: Bottling a Star: The Race to Put Fusion on the Grid
item.description: Fusion power has been thirty years away for sixty years. But in Everett, Washington, Helion Energy is building machines that smash rings of plasma together at one hundred fifty million degrees, and Microsoft already signed a contract to buy the electricity. In the premiere of The Prototype, Alden Isaac goes inside the race to bottle a star: Helion's fifty-megawatt Orion plant rising in Malaga, Washington, MIT spinoff Commonwealth Fusion's SPARC reactor nearing switch-on in Massachusetts, and the honest physics and engineering hurdles, from neutron-shredded walls to tritium shortages, standing between the workshop and the grid.
